content_voiceover: Even though specific assays exist, DOAC monitoring remains genuinely problematic in practice, and this slide outlines why. First, we lack validated expected therapeutic plasma concentrations for these drugs. Unlike warfarin, where decades of data gave us a clear INR target range of two to three for most indications, DOACs were developed and approved using fixed dosing strategies that did not require routine monitoring, so there is no established therapeutic window to compare a measured level against. Second, we do not have solid data linking specific plasma concentrations to increased thrombotic risk on one end or increased hemorrhagic risk on the other, so even if you get a number back, it is often unclear what to do with it clinically. Third, there is no standardization across laboratories, different assay platforms, reagents, and calibrators can give different results for the same sample, making it hard to compare values between institutions or trust a single cutoff. Together these limitations are exactly why routine DOAC monitoring is not recommended for most patients, and testing is reserved for specific scenarios like active bleeding, urgent surgery, renal impairment, extremes of body weight, suspected overdose, or questionable adherence.
keypoints: No validated therapeutic plasma concentration range exists for DOACs
Unclear which drug levels correlate with bleeding versus thrombosis risk
Assay methods and calibrators are not standardized across laboratories
Routine monitoring is reserved for specific clinical scenarios, not all patients
keypoint_voiceover: DOACs have no validated therapeutic plasma range the way warfarin has an INR target. It is unclear which levels correlate with bleeding versus thrombosis risk, and assay methods aren't standardized across labs. So routine monitoring is reserved for specific situations, not used for every patient.
